newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian campaigner slams Belarus record on rights.
newsitem.headline: Russian campaigner slams Belarus record on rights.

text.p: A leading Russian human rights campaigner on Thursday criticised a Union Treaty between Moscow and Belarus and accused the Kremlin of turning a blind eye to a lack of democracy in the neighbouring Slav state.

Yelena Bonner, widow of Soviet dissident and Nobel Peace laureate Andrei Sakharov, said Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko was smothering democracy in his former Soviet republic and Moscow should do more to defend democracy there.
"We must find ways to preserve and protect the shoots of democracy in Russia. In Minsk the shoots are weaker and Lukashenko is smothering them completely," Bonner told a news conference.

"What is absolutely impermissible is the Russian leadership's silence about all the undemocratic actions by the Belarus state apparatus, the president and the government. It is a full deviation from the defence of democratic principles."

Lukashenko has been alienated by Western governments who accuse him of using authoritarian methods. He has cracked down on the media, taken on sweeping powers, dissolved parliament and shown little tolerance for opposition.

Baton-wielding police clashed on Wednesday with marchers protesting in Minsk against the diluted Union Treaty which Lukashenko signed earlier in the day with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Moscow.

Belarus Foreign Minister Ivan Antonovich, speaking at a news conference in Minsk accused reporters of waging "an information war" against Lukashenko and said accreditation rules for the media would be tightened.
He also advised correspondents not to attend unsanctioned meetings.

Russian leaders have largely steered clear of the human rights issue in forging links with Lukashenko, although the Kremlin expressed concern last month over the crackdown on Russian reporters and other journalists in Minsk.

Bonner said the Union Treaty, which was watered down at the request of Russian liberals to limit its practical implications and ensure sovereignty for both states, had been negotiated in secrecy behind the backs of the Russian people.
"The Russian leadership, in that sense, has cheated us," she said.
The London-based human rights organisation Amnesty International on Thursday urged the Russian authorities to do more to tidy up their own human rights record.
It issued a report condemning what it called widespread, systematic use of torture by Russia's security forces and said new legislation and older Soviet-era laws encouraged abuses.

"Under the guise of fighting crime, the Russian Federation has expanded the powers of security and law enforcement agencies to the detriment of constitutional rights, and members of ethnic minorities are particularly vulnerable," Amnesty said.
Amnesty said its report also described conditions of detention in Russia as "amounting to torture".

Amnesty said it had received reports that prisoners die from overcrowding, lack of oxygen and poor conditions. Cases of death from lack of oxygen had taken place in almost all large pre-trial detention centres in Russia, it said.
"It is clearly within the power of the Russian authorities to eliminate these illegal practices," Amnesty said.
